back: Staphylococcus aureus, producing an acute destructive endocarditis with in-hospital mortality around 20 to 25 percent.

front: What did the 2023 Duke-ISCVID revision add to the major imaging criteria for endocarditis?
back: 18F-FDG PET/CT metabolic activity around prosthetic valves or devices and cardiac CT findings now qualify, alongside echocardiographic evidence, plus a surgical inspection major criterion.

front: Which serologic result is a major Duke criterion for Q fever endocarditis?
back: Coxiella burnetii phase I IgG titer of 1:800 or greater; treatment is doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for at least 18 months.

front: What endocarditis pathogen requires colonoscopy in every case?
back: Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis), because of its strong association with colonic neoplasia.

front: What is the preferred regimen for E. faecalis native valve endocarditis and why?
back: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone for 6 weeks; ceftriaxone saturates complementary penicillin-binding proteins for synergy, matching ampicillin-gentamicin cure rates without nephrotoxicity.

front: What did the POET trial establish for endocarditis treatment?
back: In stable left-sided endocarditis with susceptible organisms and no abscess, oral step-down after at least 10 days of IV therapy was noninferior to continued IV treatment.

front: When is rifampin added in staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis?
back: After blood cultures clear, to penetrate biofilm on prosthetic material while avoiding resistance selection during active bacteremia; gentamicin accompanies the first 2 weeks.

front: What does new PR prolongation signify in aortic valve endocarditis?
back: Aortic root or annular abscess extending toward the atrioventricular node, a form of uncontrolled infection that is a surgical indication.

front: How is cardiac implantable electronic device infection managed?
back: Complete extraction of the generator and all leads regardless of which component appears infected, with reimplantation deferred until blood cultures are negative at least 72 hours.

front: What are the three canonical surgical indications in left-sided endocarditis?
back: Heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteremia), and embolism prevention with vegetations over 10 mm plus embolic events.

front: What short-course therapy is validated for uncomplicated right-sided MSSA endocarditis?
back: Two weeks of an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam; vancomycin is not reliable in 2-week regimens, so MRSA disease receives standard durations.

front: Which cardiac conditions still warrant endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures?
back: Prosthetic valves or repair material, prior endocarditis, unrepaired or incompletely repaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, and transplant valvulopathy; amoxicillin 2 g is standard.

front: What is Lemierre syndrome?
back: Fusobacterium necrophorum septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after oropharyngeal infection in a young patient, with septic pulmonary emboli.

front: Which organism has a specific affinity for infecting the atherosclerotic aorta?
back: Salmonella; infected (mycotic) aortic aneurysms require surgical or endovascular source control plus prolonged antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.

front: Why does endocarditis produce continuous rather than intermittent bacteremia?
back: The vegetation sheds organisms directly into flowing blood, so three separate blood culture sets before antibiotics are positive in most untreated patients.

front: What is nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis?
back: Sterile platelet-fibrin vegetations in malignancy (classically mucinous adenocarcinoma) or severe illness, presenting with emboli and negative cultures; treated with anticoagulation.

front: Why are antibiotics and antimotility agents avoided in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection?
back: Antibiotics induce phage-encoded Shiga toxin production and are associated with increased hemolytic uremic syndrome risk; antimotility agents retain toxin in the colon.

front: When is nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis treated with antibiotics?
back: Severe disease, age over 50, prosthetic or endovascular material, hemoglobinopathy, and immunocompromise; healthy adults are not treated because antibiotics prolong carriage.

front: What does vomiting 1 to 6 hours after a meal indicate in foodborne illness?
back: A preformed toxin ingested with the food: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin or Bacillus cereus emetic toxin (cereulide), classically from fried rice.

front: What is the diagnostic threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
back: Ascitic fluid absolute polymorphonuclear count of 250 cells per cubic millimeter or greater; treat 5 days with cefotaxime or ceftriaxone even if culture is negative.

front: What adjunct reduces renal failure and mortality in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
back: Intravenous albumin, 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3, clearest with creatinine above 1 mg/dL or bilirubin above 4 mg/dL.

front: What ascitic findings suggest secondary rather than spontaneous peritonitis?
back: Very high PMN counts, multiple organisms or anaerobes, protein above 1 g/dL, glucose below 50 mg/dL, or LDH above serum; obtain CT for a surgical source.

front: What did the STOP-IT trial show about antibiotic duration in intra-abdominal infection?
back: After adequate source control, roughly 4 days of antibiotics achieved outcomes equivalent to longer symptom-guided courses.

front: What does Tokyo Grade III (severe) cholangitis require?
back: Emergent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP, because organ dysfunction with pus under pressure does not respond to antibiotics alone.

front: What is the modern intervention strategy for infected pancreatic necrosis?
back: Delay intervention toward 4 weeks for walled-off necrosis when possible, then step-up: percutaneous or endoscopic drainage first, minimally invasive necrosectomy only for failure (PANTER trial).

front: What complication pattern defines hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess?
back: Cryptogenic monomicrobial abscess in diabetics (capsular types K1/K2) with metastatic endophthalmitis and CNS infection; visual symptoms demand same-day ophthalmology.

front: How does treatment of amebic liver abscess differ from pyogenic abscess?
back: Amebic abscess responds to metronidazole followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin) and rarely needs drainage; pyogenic abscess requires percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics.

front: What did the CODA trial show for uncomplicated appendicitis?
back: Antibiotics were noninferior to appendectomy at 30 days, but nearly a third crossed to surgery by 90 days, and appendicolith predicted medical failure.

front: What is first-line H. pylori therapy in North America and its follow-up?
back: Bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, tetracycline, metronidazole) for 14 days, with mandatory eradication testing by breath or stool at least 4 weeks after completion.

front: What is the diagnostic finding and treatment of Whipple disease?
back: Duodenal biopsy with PAS-positive foamy macrophages confirmed by PCR; ceftriaxone for 2 weeks then trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for about a year.

front: How is CMV colitis diagnosed in an immunocompromised patient?
back: Tissue diagnosis: colonoscopic biopsy showing inclusion-bearing cells with positive immunohistochemistry; plasma PCR alone neither confirms nor excludes colitis.

front: What are the only two indications to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria?
back: Pregnancy and upcoming endoscopic urologic procedures with expected mucosal bleeding; treatment elsewhere causes harm without benefit.

front: What are the three first-line agents for uncomplicated cystitis?
back: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength twice daily for 3 days, and fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose.

front: Why is nitrofurantoin never used for pyelonephritis?
back: It concentrates only in urine and never achieves adequate tissue levels; it is also avoided when creatinine clearance falls below roughly 30 mL/min.

front: What does persistent fever at 48 to 72 hours of appropriate pyelonephritis therapy require?
back: CT imaging for obstruction, perinephric or renal abscess, or emphysematous infection; an obstructed infected kidney needs emergent stent or nephrostomy decompression.

front: How is emphysematous pyelonephritis managed?
back: Resuscitation, carbapenem-level antibiotics, and urgent percutaneous drainage, reserving nephrectomy for extensive gas, nonresponse, or destroyed parenchyma; it occurs almost exclusively in diabetics.

front: Why does chronic bacterial prostatitis require 4 to 6 weeks of a fluoroquinolone?
back: The uninflamed prostate is a pharmacologic sanctuary that only lipophilic, favorably ionized drugs penetrate; it presents as recurrent same-organism UTIs in a man.

front: What nonantibiotic prophylaxis was noninferior to daily antibiotics for recurrent UTI in the ALTAR trial?
back: Methenamine hippurate, which liberates formaldehyde in acidic urine; vaginal estrogen is the other key nonantibiotic option in postmenopausal women.

front: What is the current first-line treatment for gonorrhea?
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose (1 g if 150 kg or more), without routine azithromycin; add doxycycline only for documented or untested chlamydial coinfection.

front: Which gonococcal infection site requires routine test of cure?
back: Pharyngeal gonorrhea, tested at 7 to 14 days, because it is the hardest site to eradicate; all patients are also retested for reinfection at about 3 months.

front: Why did doxycycline replace azithromycin as first-line chlamydia treatment?
back: Randomized data showed azithromycin inferior at rectal sites, where infection is common and often unrecognized; doxycycline runs 7 days, or 21 days for LGV.

front: What is the empiric treatment sequence for Mycoplasma genitalium without resistance testing?
back: Doxycycline for 7 days to lower organism load, followed immediately by moxifloxacin for 7 days; beta-lactams are useless because the organism has no cell wall.

front: What is the current outpatient regimen for pelvic inflammatory disease?
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once, plus doxycycline and metronidazole each for 14 days, with clinical reassessment at 72 hours.

front: What is doxy-PEP and its evidence?
back: Doxycycline 200 mg within 72 hours after condomless sex reduced bacterial STIs by roughly two thirds (chlamydia and syphilis) in trials of MSM and transgender women with prior STI.

front: How does daily valacyclovir suppression change genital herpes outcomes?
back: It reduces recurrences by about three quarters and transmission to susceptible partners by about half, proven in a discordant-couples trial.

front: How does pyelonephritis of a transplanted kidney present differently?
back: The allograft is denervated, so infection presents as fever, graft tenderness, or unexplained creatinine rise rather than classic flank pain.

front: What organisms cause nonpurulent cellulitis versus purulent skin infection?
back: Nonpurulent cellulitis is overwhelmingly beta-hemolytic streptococci, treated with cephalexin or cefazolin; abscesses are S. aureus, often MRSA, and require drainage.

front: Do drained skin abscesses need antibiotics?
back: Yes, randomized trials showed adjunctive trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin after incision and drainage improves cure and reduces recurrence.

front: What prophylaxis reduces recurrent leg cellulitis?
back: Penicillin V 250 mg twice daily halved recurrences in the PATCH I trial; also treat tinea pedis and use compression for edema.

front: Can the LRINEC score exclude necrotizing soft tissue infection?
back: No; its sensitivity is inadequate as a rule-out test, and operative exploration on clinical suspicion is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic act.

front: Why is clindamycin added in necrotizing streptococcal infection?
back: It suppresses toxin and superantigen production and retains activity against high-inoculum, stationary-phase streptococci where beta-lactams falter (the Eagle effect).

front: Why is amoxicillin-clavulanate the drug of choice for bite wounds?
back: It covers Pasteurella multocida, Eikenella corrodens, anaerobes, and skin flora together; cephalexin and clindamycin each miss Pasteurella and Eikenella.

front: Which bite-associated organism causes fulminant sepsis in asplenic patients?
back: Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dog bites, producing overwhelming sepsis with purpura fulminans in asplenic and cirrhotic hosts.

front: What infection follows saltwater exposure in a cirrhotic patient, and how is it treated?
back: Vibrio vulnificus necrotizing infection with hemorrhagic bullae; treat with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and early surgical debridement.

front: What exposure and treatment characterize Mycobacterium marinum infection?
back: Fish tank or fish-handling exposure causing indolent nodular or sporotrichoid hand lesions; treat for months with clarithromycin plus ethambutol or rifampin.

front: What bedside findings make diabetic foot osteomyelitis probable?
back: A positive probe-to-bone test, ulcer over 2 square centimeters, ESR above 70, and radiographic cortical erosion; bone biopsy is the diagnostic anchor.

front: When are antibiotics started in stable native vertebral osteomyelitis with negative blood cultures?
back: Only after image-guided biopsy obtains a microbiologic diagnosis; empiric therapy first suppresses culture yield and commits to guess-directed treatment.

front: What antibiotic duration is standard for pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis?
back: Six weeks, shown noninferior to 12 weeks in a randomized French trial, extended for undrained abscess or resistant organisms.

front: When is DAIR appropriate for prosthetic joint infection?
back: Early postoperative or acute hematogenous infection with short symptom duration and a stable implant; modular components are exchanged and staphylococcal cases get rifampin combination therapy.

front: What synovial fluid white count suggests native joint septic arthritis?
back: Above 50,000 cells per microliter with neutrophil predominance makes infection likely, above 100,000 very likely; crystals in the fluid do not exclude coexisting infection.

front: What triad characterizes disseminated gonococcal infection?
back: Tenosynovitis, dermatitis (scattered pustular lesions), and migratory polyarthralgia; joint and blood cultures are often negative, so mucosal site NAATs carry the diagnostic yield.

front: Which coreceptor does most transmitted HIV use for entry, and which drug blocks it?
back: CCR5 is the coreceptor of most transmitted (R5) virus. Maraviroc blocks CCR5 and requires a tropism assay before use.

front: What laboratory pattern defines acute HIV infection on the CDC testing algorithm?
back: A reactive fourth generation antigen-antibody screen with a negative or indeterminate HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay and detectable HIV RNA.

front: What test must return before any patient receives abacavir, and why?
back: HLA-B*5701 testing. Carriers are at risk for a systemic hypersensitivity reaction that can be fatal on rechallenge; screening essentially abolishes it.

front: What does the M184V mutation do to lamivudine, viral fitness, and tenofovir susceptibility?
back: It confers high-level lamivudine and emtricitabine resistance while crippling replicative fitness and increasing susceptibility to tenofovir and zidovudine.

front: Which reverse transcriptase mutation is selected by tenofovir failure?
back: K65R, which reduces susceptibility to tenofovir, abacavir, and lamivudine but increases zidovudine susceptibility; it is antagonistic with M184V.

front: Name the three conditions that must be excluded before using the dolutegravir plus lamivudine two-drug regimen.
back: Baseline viral load above 500,000 copies per milliliter, chronic hepatitis B coinfection, and absence of baseline genotype (or transmitted resistance) results.

front: Why do dolutegravir, bictegravir, and cobicistat raise serum creatinine without harming the kidney?
back: They inhibit tubular creatinine secretion (OCT2 or MATE1), causing a benign rise of roughly 0.1 to 0.15 milligrams per deciliter with unchanged true glomerular filtration.

front: How does tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) toxicity differ from tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)?
back: TDF causes proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome) and bone density loss; TAF has less renal and bone toxicity but more weight gain and lipid elevation.

front: What is the U=U message and its evidence base?
back: Undetectable equals untransmittable: durable viral suppression below 200 copies per milliliter eliminates sexual HIV transmission, shown by HPTN 052 and the PARTNER studies.

front: What is the window for starting HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and how long does it last?
back: Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure; continue a three-drug regimen (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir or raltegravir) for 28 days.

front: Which long-acting injectable PrEP agent beat daily oral tenofovir-based PrEP in HPTN 083 and 084?
back: Cabotegravir, given intramuscularly every two months, largely because it removes the daily adherence requirement.

front: Why must integrase inhibitors be separated from antacids and mineral supplements?
back: Polyvalent cations (calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron) chelate INSTIs in the gut, lowering absorption enough to cause virologic failure.

front: What adjustment does rifampin force on an integrase-inhibitor-based HIV regimen?
back: Rifampin induction requires dolutegravir twice daily and prohibits bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, and boosted regimens; rifabutin is the alternative rifamycin.

front: What is the preferred anchor class and example regimens for first-line HIV therapy?
back: Second generation integrase inhibitors: bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine, dolutegravir plus a tenofovir backbone, or dolutegravir plus lamivudine when eligibility conditions are met.

front: Which HIV regimens are preferred in pregnancy and what determines intrapartum management?
back: Dolutegravir-based therapy with a tenofovir plus emtricitabine or lamivudine backbone; viral load near delivery decides mode of delivery and intravenous zidovudine (above 1,000 copies: cesarean plus zidovudine).

front: At what CD4 thresholds do Pneumocystis, Toxoplasma, Cryptococcus, CMV, and MAC classically appear?
back: Pneumocystis below 200; Toxoplasma and Cryptococcus below 100; cytomegalovirus end-organ disease and disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex below 50.

front: What are the criteria for adjunctive corticosteroids in HIV-associated Pneumocystis pneumonia?
back: Room air arterial oxygen tension below 70 mmHg or an alveolar-arterial gradient of 35 or more; give prednisone within 72 hours of starting treatment.

front: When is Pneumocystis prophylaxis started and stopped in HIV?
back: Start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole at CD4 below 200, CD4 percentage under 14, or with oropharyngeal candidiasis; stop after the count exceeds 200 for at least three months on suppressive therapy.

front: How is toxoplasmic encephalitis distinguished from primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS?
back: Toxoplasmosis: multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions in a seropositive patient responding to empiric therapy in 10 to 14 days. Lymphoma: solitary periventricular lesion, positive CSF EBV PCR, thallium or FDG avidity.

front: Outline the three phases of cryptococcal meningitis treatment in HIV.
back: Induction: liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks. Consolidation: fluconazole 800 mg daily for 8 weeks. Maintenance: fluconazole 200 mg daily for at least a year and until immune reconstitution.

front: How is raised intracranial pressure managed in cryptococcal meningitis?
back: Serial therapeutic lumbar punctures for pressures of 25 cm of water or more with symptoms, removing enough CSF to halve the opening pressure; corticosteroids do not help.

front: When should ART start after diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis, and why?
back: Defer 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungals; the COAT trial showed earlier initiation increased mortality from intracranial immune reconstitution inflammation.

front: What are the ART timing rules in HIV-tuberculosis coinfection?
back: Start ART within 2 weeks of TB treatment when CD4 is below 50, within 8 weeks otherwise; delay toward 8 weeks in tuberculous meningitis.

front: What is the classic laboratory and clinical fingerprint of disseminated MAC?
back: CD4 below 50 with fever, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and a markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase; diagnose by mycobacterial blood culture.

front: Why is MAC primary prophylaxis no longer routinely given?
back: Since 2019, patients who immediately start effective ART do not benefit; prophylaxis (weekly azithromycin) is reserved for those not on suppressive therapy.

front: How is sight-threatening CMV retinitis treated?
back: Oral valganciclovir induction then maintenance, plus immediate intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet injections for lesions near the fovea or optic nerve; continue until CD4 exceeds 100 for 3 to 6 months.

front: Define paradoxical versus unmasking IRIS.
back: Paradoxical IRIS worsens a known treated infection after ART starts; unmasking IRIS reveals a previously subclinical infection in an exaggerated inflammatory form.

front: What are the three management rules for IRIS?
back: Continue ART (except life-threatening CNS disease), continue treatment of the opportunistic infection, and treat inflammation with NSAIDs or corticosteroids for severe disease.

front: Which vaccines are contraindicated below a CD4 count of 200?
back: Live vaccines: measles-mumps-rubella and varicella; also avoid live attenuated influenza and oral typhoid. Nonliving vaccines including recombinant zoster remain safe.

front: What screening test belongs on the admission panel of every patient with a CD4 count of 100 or below?
back: Serum cryptococcal antigen; antigenemia precedes meningitis by weeks, and a positive result mandates lumbar puncture with preemptive fluconazole if meningitis is excluded.

front: What is the immediate management rule for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis?
back: Start intravenous acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at the moment of suspicion, before PCR confirmation; continue 14 to 21 days.

front: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?
back: Varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion: facial paralysis, ear pain, and vesicles in the auditory canal or on the auricle, treated with antivirals plus corticosteroids.

front: What is VZV vasculopathy and when should it be suspected?
back: Viral invasion of cerebral arteries causing stroke weeks to months after zoster, classically contralateral hemiparesis after ophthalmic zoster; CSF shows pleocytosis with VZV antibody or PCR, treated with intravenous acyclovir.

front: Which donor-recipient CMV serostatus pairing carries the highest risk in solid organ transplantation?
back: Seropositive donor into seronegative recipient (D+/R-), because the recipient has no preexisting CMV immunity; in stem cell transplant the seropositive recipient is highest risk.

front: Contrast UL97 and UL54 mutations in cytomegalovirus resistance.
back: UL97 kinase mutations block ganciclovir's first phosphorylation and confer ganciclovir resistance only; UL54 polymerase mutations can extend resistance to foscarnet and cidofovir.

front: What is letermovir's target and clinical niche?
back: It inhibits the CMV terminase complex (UL56) and is used for prophylaxis in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation because it spares the marrow.

front: How reliable is heterophile antibody testing for infectious mononucleosis?
back: It misses roughly 10 to 15 percent of adult cases and many early cases; EBV viral capsid antigen IgM settles ambiguous ones, and EBNA antibodies exclude acute infection.

front: What is post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder and its stepwise management?
back: EBV-driven B cell proliferation when T cell surveillance is suppressed after transplant; manage with reduction of immunosuppression, rituximab for CD20-positive disease, then chemotherapy or EBV-specific T cells.

front: What does parvovirus B19 cause in patients with sickle cell disease and in the immunocompromised?
back: Transient aplastic crisis with reticulocytes near zero in hemolytic states; chronic pure red cell aplasia in the immunocompromised, diagnosed by serum PCR and treated with intravenous immunoglobulin.

front: What is measles immune amnesia?
back: Measles depletes preexisting antibody repertoires and memory lymphocytes, leaving survivors more vulnerable to other infections for two to three years.

front: Give the meaning of HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HBc.
back: HBsAg means current infection; anti-HBs means immunity from resolved infection or vaccination; anti-HBc means true exposure to the virus (IgM acute, IgG lifelong).

front: Who must be screened for hepatitis B before rituximab, and what is done for those at risk?
back: Everyone: check HBsAg and anti-HBc. Give prophylactic entecavir or tenofovir to those at meaningful reactivation risk, including HBsAg-negative anti-HBc-positive patients receiving anti-CD20 therapy.

front: Name the pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral combinations that cure most hepatitis C.
back: Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir and glecaprevir-pibrentasvir, given 8 to 12 weeks, achieve sustained virologic response in more than 95 percent.

front: Which hepatitis virus is most lethal in third trimester pregnancy?
back: Hepatitis E genotype 1, with maternal mortality reported at 20 to 25 percent in endemic regions; genotype 3 causes chronic hepatitis in transplant recipients, treatable with ribavirin.

front: When does dengue become dangerous and what are key warning signs?
back: At defervescence (days 4 to 7), when plasma leak begins; warning signs include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, and rising hematocrit with falling platelets.

front: What is first-line therapy for candidemia and the two nondrug steps that accompany it?
back: An echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin), removal of central venous catheters when feasible, and daily blood cultures; treat 14 days from the first negative culture.

front: What makes Candida auris an urgent public health threat?
back: Frequent multidrug resistance, misidentification by older biochemical systems, persistent skin colonization, environmental contamination, and healthcare outbreaks requiring contact precautions.

front: What do the halo sign and air crescent sign indicate in a neutropenic patient?
back: The halo sign (nodule ringed by ground-glass hemorrhage) is early invasive aspergillosis; the air crescent appears later with neutrophil recovery as necrotic lung retracts.

front: What is first-line therapy for invasive aspergillosis and its monitoring requirement?
back: Voriconazole, with therapeutic drug monitoring targeting troughs of roughly 1 to 5.5 micrograms per milliliter; isavuconazole is the principal alternative.

front: Which hosts are classically predisposed to mucormycosis, and why does ketoacidosis matter?
back: Diabetic ketoacidosis, iron overload and deferoxamine use, neutropenia, and high-dose steroids; acidosis liberates iron from transferrin, feeding the fungus's iron uptake system.

front: What are the four pillars of mucormycosis treatment?
back: Urgent repeated surgical debridement, high-dose liposomal amphotericin B, reversal of the underlying predisposition, and isavuconazole or posaconazole for step-down or salvage.

front: Contrast the hyphae of Aspergillus and the Mucorales on histopathology.
back: Aspergillus: narrow, regularly septate hyphae branching at acute angles. Mucorales: broad, ribbon-like, sparsely septate hyphae branching at right angles.

front: Which invasive fungi are missed by beta-D-glucan testing?
back: Cryptococcus (the capsule masks it) and the Mucorales (their wall largely lacks it); a negative glucan with radiographic mold disease should raise mucormycosis suspicion.

front: What is the fastest diagnostic test for disseminated histoplasmosis?
back: Urine (and serum) Histoplasma antigen testing, which is most sensitive precisely in disseminated disease; severe disease gets amphotericin then a year of itraconazole.

front: What is distinctive about coccidioidal meningitis in CSF findings and treatment duration?
back: It can show eosinophilic pleocytosis, and fluconazole must continue lifelong because relapse follows discontinuation; hydrocephalus is a common complication.

front: How does Pneumocystis pneumonia differ between HIV and non-HIV immunosuppressed hosts?
back: Non-HIV disease is abrupt and fulminant with fewer organisms, more inflammation, and higher mortality; HIV disease is indolent with high organism burdens.

front: Which patients on corticosteroids warrant Pneumocystis prophylaxis?
back: Those on roughly 20 mg of prednisone daily or more for a month or longer combined with another immunosuppressive agent, plus transplant recipients and patients on agents like alemtuzumab.

front: Name the signature toxicities of voriconazole.
back: Hepatotoxicity, transient visual disturbances, photosensitivity with long-term skin cancer risk, periostitis from fluoride accumulation, and neurotoxicity at high troughs; kinetics are nonlinear with CYP2C19 variation.

front: Why is flucytosine never used alone, and what monitoring does it need?
back: Resistance emerges rapidly on monotherapy; it partners amphotericin for cryptococcal induction and needs level monitoring because it causes marrow suppression, especially in renal impairment.

front: Which mold causes positive blood cultures with necrotic skin lesions in neutropenia, and which is linked to near-drowning brain abscesses?
back: Fusarium sporulates in tissue and grows in blood cultures with skin lesions; Scedosporium apiospermum causes brain abscesses after near-drowning and is amphotericin resistant (use voriconazole).

front: What defines severe malaria and what is its treatment?
back: Falciparum (or knowlesi) with impaired consciousness, acidosis, kidney injury, respiratory distress, hypoglycemia, severe anemia, or parasitemia of roughly 5 percent or more in the nonimmune; treat with intravenous artesunate.

front: Which malaria species form hypnozoites and what is required before radical cure?
back: Plasmodium vivax and ovale; G6PD testing is mandatory before primaquine (14 days) or single-dose tafenoquine, both of which hemolyze G6PD-deficient patients and are contraindicated in pregnancy.

front: Compare the post-travel continuation of atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline prophylaxis.
back: Atovaquone-proguanil continues 7 days after leaving the endemic area; doxycycline continues 4 weeks, because only atovaquone-proguanil kills liver-stage parasites.

front: How is chronic Chagas disease diagnosed and who gets benznidazole?
back: Two different concordant serologic assays; treat acute, congenital, and reactivated disease, and chronic infection in patients under about 50 without advanced cardiomyopathy.

front: What is the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in the United States?
back: Liposomal amphotericin B; miltefosine is an oral alternative for selected disease but is teratogenic. Visceral leishmaniasis relapses in advanced HIV.

front: Why must Entamoeba histolytica treatment always include two drugs?
back: Metronidazole or tinidazole kills invasive trophozoites but not intestinal cysts; a luminal agent such as paromomycin must follow or the patient can relapse and transmit.

front: How is Entamoeba histolytica distinguished from Entamoeba dispar?
back: Microscopy cannot separate them; stool antigen testing or PCR specific for histolytica, or serology in liver abscess, establishes true infection.

front: What triggers Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome and what is its classic triad?
back: Corticosteroids above all, plus HTLV-1 coinfection and transplant immunosuppression; the triad is gram-negative bacteremia, ileus or abdominal symptoms, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, often without eosinophilia.

front: What screening rule prevents Strongyloides hyperinfection?
back: Send Strongyloides IgG serology (or give empiric ivermectin) before significant corticosteroid therapy or transplantation in anyone who has lived in an endemic region, including the southeastern United States.

front: What is Katayama fever and why are egg studies negative during it?
back: Acute schistosomiasis 4 to 8 weeks after heavy freshwater exposure: fever, urticaria, cough, and marked eosinophilia occurring before worms mature to egg production, so stool and urine microscopy are still negative.

front: How is viable parenchymal neurocysticercosis treated?
back: Albendazole (adding praziquantel for multiple cysts) under corticosteroid cover plus antiepileptics; calcified lesions get antiepileptics alone, and steroids require prior tuberculosis and Strongyloides screening.

front: Why is Loa loa microfilaremia quantified before ivermectin in parts of Central Africa?
back: In heavily coinfected patients, ivermectin can precipitate fatal encephalopathy from massive microfilarial killing, so loads are measured before mass onchocerciasis treatment.

front: Which infections classically cause eosinophilia in a returned traveler, and which do not?
back: Tissue-migrating helminths (acute schistosomiasis, trichinellosis, hookworm and Ascaris migration, Strongyloides, filariae) cause it; protozoa such as malaria, Giardia, and Entamoeba do not, with Cystoisospora the exception.

front: What are the timing and key contraindications of yellow fever vaccination?
back: Give at an authorized center at least 10 days before travel; contraindicated under 6 months of age, in thymus disorders, and significant immunosuppression, with caution for first doses after age 60.

front: What incubation rule helps exclude dengue in a returned traveler?
back: Dengue incubates 4 to 14 days, so fever beginning more than two weeks after leaving an endemic area is effectively not dengue; falciparum malaria usually presents within a month of exposure.

front: What PK/PD index drives beta-lactam efficacy, and what is the clinical implication in critically ill patients?
back: Time above MIC (fT>MIC). Prolonged or continuous infusions raise fT>MIC in patients with augmented renal clearance without changing the total daily dose.

front: What is the consensus vancomycin exposure target for serious MRSA infection?
back: An AUC/MIC of 400 to 600, guided by measured levels (Bayesian or two-level methods), replacing trough targets of 15 to 20 mg/L.

front: Why can daptomycin never treat pneumonia, and what infection with lung lesions can it still treat?
back: Pulmonary surfactant inactivates it in the alveolus. It remains effective for hematogenous septic pulmonary emboli from right-sided endocarditis.

front: What laboratory monitoring does daptomycin require, and what co-medication should be held?
back: Baseline and weekly creatine phosphokinase (CPK) for skeletal muscle toxicity; hold statins during therapy when feasible.

front: Name the three principal toxicity classes of linezolid and their mechanisms.
back: Serotonin syndrome (weak MAO inhibition with serotonergic drugs), reversible thrombocytopenia beyond about 2 weeks, and optic or peripheral neuropathy with lactic acidosis from mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition on prolonged use.

front: What three properties make once-daily aminoglycoside dosing effective and safer?
back: Concentration-dependent killing (high Cmax/MIC), a prolonged post-antibiotic effect covering the trough, and saturable renal and cochlear uptake that a drug-free interval offloads.

front: Which inherited variant causes profound deafness after even brief aminoglycoside exposure?
back: The maternally inherited mitochondrial m.1555A>G variant in MT-RNR1, which makes human 12S rRNA resemble the bacterial ribosomal target.

front: List the FDA boxed warnings for fluoroquinolones.
back: Tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, and exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, with additional warnings for aortic aneurysm and dissection, dysglycemia, and QT prolongation.

front: By what two renal mechanisms does trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alter potassium and creatinine?
back: Trimethoprim blocks the distal nephron epithelial sodium channel (amiloride-like) causing hyperkalemia, and inhibits tubular creatinine secretion, raising creatinine 10 to 20 percent without a true GFR change.

front: What drives penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity, and why is cefazolin usually safe in penicillin allergy?
back: Shared R1 side chains, not the beta-lactam ring; overall cross-reactivity is roughly 1 to 2 percent, and cefazolin has a unique side chain shared with no penicillin.

front: Which single beta-lactam pairing shows true aztreonam cross-reactivity?
back: Ceftazidime, because aztreonam and ceftazidime share an identical side chain; aztreonam is otherwise safe in severe penicillin allergy.

front: Why is cefepime preferred over ceftriaxone for serious Enterobacter cloacae infection despite reported ceftriaxone susceptibility?
back: Enterobacter carries inducible chromosomal AmpC; third-generation cephalosporins select stably derepressed AmpC mutants on therapy, while cefepime is stable to AmpC.

front: What positive D-test result means for clindamycin therapy?
back: The isolate carries inducible erm methylase; clindamycin monotherapy will select constitutive resistance and fail, so choose another agent.

front: Why do dalbavancin and ertapenem suit outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy?
back: Dalbavancin's roughly 8 to 10 day half-life allows single or two-dose regimens, and ertapenem's high protein binding permits once-daily dosing, including for ESBL organisms.

front: Which commonly used antibacterials need no renal dose adjustment?
back: Nafcillin and oxacillin, ceftriaxone, doxycycline, tigecycline, azithromycin, clindamycin, linezolid, metronidazole, and moxifloxacin (which also fails in urine).

front: How does MRSA resist beta-lactams, and how does VRE resist vancomycin?
back: MRSA expresses PBP2a from mecA on the SCCmec cassette, a low-affinity transpeptidase; VRE rebuilds its precursor terminus to D-alanyl-D-lactate under the vanA or vanB operons.

front: What did the MERINO trial establish for ESBL bloodstream infection?
back: Piperacillin-tazobactam failed to prove noninferiority to meropenem, with mortality favoring meropenem, so carbapenems are standard for serious ESBL bacteremia.

front: Match the three major carbapenemase families to active agents.
back: KPC: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, or imipenem-relebactam. NDM (metallo): ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam, or cefiderocol. OXA-48: ceftazidime-avibactam or cefiderocol.

front: Why does combining ceftazidime-avibactam with aztreonam work against NDM producers?
back: NDM cannot hydrolyze aztreonam, and avibactam neutralizes the co-carried serine beta-lactamases that would otherwise destroy aztreonam.

front: How does cefiderocol enter gram-negative bacteria?
back: It is a siderophore cephalosporin carried through the outer membrane by bacterial iron transporters, bypassing porin loss and surviving metallo-beta-lactamase hydrolysis.

front: What is the current first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea in the United States?
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once (1 g at 150 kg or more); azithromycin co-treatment was dropped in 2020, with doxycycline added only for chlamydial coverage.

front: Name the seven CDC Core Elements of hospital antibiotic stewardship.
back: Leadership commitment, accountability, pharmacy expertise, action, tracking, reporting, and education.

front: What are the two foundational stewardship interventions and their trade-offs?
back: Prospective audit and feedback (preserves autonomy, teaches, acts after 48 to 72 hours) and preauthorization (controls before the first dose but adds work and possible delay).

front: Give the evidence-based short durations for CAP, VAP, gram-negative bacteremia, and intra-abdominal infection.
back: CAP 5 days with early response, VAP 7 days, uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia 7 days, and 4 days after adequate source control for intra-abdominal infection (STOP-IT).

front: What is the negative predictive value use of the MRSA nasal PCR in stewardship?
back: A negative nasal MRSA PCR has a negative predictive value above 95 percent for MRSA pneumonia and is a validated trigger to stop empiric vancomycin.

front: Why is penicillin allergy delabeling a stewardship intervention?
back: About 10 percent of patients carry the label but under 1 percent are truly allergic; delabeling by history and direct oral challenge restores first-line beta-lactams and reduces MRSA, C. difficile, and surgical infections.

front: Contrast DOT and DDD as antimicrobial use metrics.
back: Days of therapy (DOT) counts each agent-day regardless of dose and is the US standard feeding the NHSN SAAR; defined daily doses (DDD) divide grams by a reference adult dose and distort pediatric and renally adjusted use.

front: What genetic elements spread resistance horizontally?
back: Conjugative plasmids carry resistance cassettes between species, transposons move genes between plasmids and chromosomes, and integrons capture and stack gene cassettes behind one promoter.

front: Why does Candida auris behave like a bacterial MDRO for infection control?
back: It colonizes skin persistently, survives on surfaces for weeks, resists azoles routinely, is misidentified by older biochemical systems, and requires contact precautions with disinfectants proven active against it; echinocandins are first-line therapy.

front: What FDA-approved microbiome products prevent recurrent C. difficile, and how?
back: A rectally administered microbiota suspension (2022) and an oral spore preparation (2023) restore colonization resistance, the gut community's suppression of pathogen expansion.

front: Which diseases require airborne precautions, and what room engineering is needed?
back: Tuberculosis, measles, varicella, and disseminated zoster (plus smallpox): fitted N95 or PAPR and a negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room exhausted outside.

front: When must soap and water replace alcohol-based hand rub?
back: C. difficile (alcohol does not kill spores), norovirus (relatively alcohol-tolerant), and visibly soiled hands.

front: List the elements of the CLABSI insertion bundle validated in the Keystone ICU project.
back: Hand hygiene, maximal sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin antisepsis, femoral site avoidance in adults, and daily review of line necessity; rates fell by about two thirds.

front: What is the dominant driver of CAUTI risk and the highest-yield intervention?
back: Catheter-days: bacteriuria accrues at roughly 3 to 7 percent per catheter-day, so nurse-driven removal protocols and avoiding placement are the key interventions.

front: State the timing, dose, and redosing rules for cefazolin surgical prophylaxis.
back: Infuse within 60 minutes before incision, 2 g (3 g at 120 kg or more), redose every 4 hours intraoperatively or after major blood loss, and stop within 24 hours of closure.

front: Which perioperative physiologic measures reduce surgical site infection?
back: Glucose below 180 to 200 mg/dL in all patients, normothermia, clippers instead of razors, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, and staphylococcal decolonization before implant surgery.

front: Why should C. difficile testing be restricted to clinically significant diarrhea?
back: 5 to 15 percent of inpatients are asymptomatic carriers, so PCR on laxative or formed stool detects colonization, creating false cases and unnecessary treatment; two-step algorithms add toxin testing to separate disease.

front: What did the REDUCE MRSA trial show about ICU decolonization?
back: Universal decolonization with chlorhexidine bathing plus nasal mupirocin beat screening-and-isolation strategies, cutting all-cause bloodstream infection by 44 percent.

front: List the core steps of an outbreak investigation.
back: Confirm the outbreak and diagnoses, write a case definition, find cases and build a line list, draw the epidemic curve, compare exposed and unexposed, test hypotheses, implement control measures early, and communicate and monitor.

front: Why did duodenoscopes transmit CRE despite guideline-compliant reprocessing?
back: The elevator mechanism harbors debris beyond the reach of brushes and high-level disinfection; the fix was engineering, disposable elevator caps and single-use scopes, not retraining.

front: What is the Spaulding classification?
back: Critical items entering sterile tissue require sterilization, semicritical items touching mucous membranes require at least high-level disinfection, and noncritical items touching intact skin require low-level disinfection.

front: State the approximate percutaneous transmission risks for HBV, HCV, and HIV after needlestick.
back: HBV up to 22 to 31 percent for clinical hepatitis from an HBeAg-positive source in the unvaccinated, HCV roughly 0.2 percent in modern surveillance, and HIV about 0.3 percent.

front: What is correct HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after an occupational needlestick?
back: A three-drug regimen (typically tenofovir-emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor) started as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72, continued for 28 days.

front: What isolation does disseminated zoster require, compared with localized zoster?
back: Disseminated zoster: airborne plus contact precautions in a negative-pressure room with nonimmune staff excluded. Localized zoster in an immunocompetent host: standard precautions with lesions covered.

front: How do NHSN surveillance definitions differ from clinical diagnosis?
back: They are deliberately objective and standardized for comparability and trending (feeding the standardized infection ratio), so a surveillance case is not automatically a clinical diagnosis and definitions must not be gamed.

front: Why do plain polysaccharide vaccines fail in infants, and how does conjugation fix this?
back: Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens giving no memory and little infant response; coupling to a carrier protein recruits T cell help, producing class-switched, boostable memory responses effective in infancy.

front: What happened to invasive Hib disease after conjugate vaccine introduction?
back: United States pediatric invasive Hib disease, roughly 20,000 cases yearly before 1988, fell by more than 99 percent.

front: What herd immunity threshold does measles require and why?
back: Roughly 92 to 95 percent immunity, because its basic reproduction number is 12 to 18; measles outbreaks are the first sign of eroding coverage.

front: What adjuvant does the recombinant zoster vaccine use, and what efficacy does it achieve?
back: AS01 (monophosphoryl lipid A plus QS-21); efficacy is roughly 97 percent at ages 50 to 69 and about 91 percent at 70 and older, given as two doses.

front: Summarize current adult pneumococcal vaccination.
back: A single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23) for pneumococcal-naive adults, routinely starting at age 50 since 2024, earlier with risk conditions.

front: Which three vaccines are standard parts of prenatal care, and when?
back: Tdap at 27 through 36 weeks every pregnancy, inactivated influenza in any trimester, and RSV vaccine at 32 through 36 weeks in season (or infant nirsevimab after birth); COVID-19 vaccination is also recommended.

front: State the timing rules for vaccination before planned immunosuppression.
back: Live vaccines at least 4 weeks before, inactivated and recombinant vaccines at least 2 weeks before; solid organ transplant recipients generally never receive live vaccines afterward.

front: What steroid dose contraindicates live vaccines?
back: Prednisone 20 mg or more daily (or 2 mg/kg) for 14 days or longer counts as high-dose immunosuppression.

front: How does rituximab affect vaccination planning?
back: B cell depletion abolishes antibody responses for roughly 6 months or more per dose, so vaccines should be given at least 2 weeks before starting or timed late in the dosing interval.

front: Should household contacts of immunocompromised patients receive live vaccines?
back: Yes: MMR, varicella, and rotavirus are recommended because vaccine strains essentially do not transmit; the caveat is avoiding diaper handling of rotavirus-vaccinated infants for 4 weeks if severely immunocompromised.

front: Name the true vaccine contraindications.
back: Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component; severe immunodeficiency or pregnancy for live vaccines; encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis vaccine; prior intussusception for rotavirus. Mild illness, antibiotics, and egg allergy are not contraindications.

front: How do VAERS and the Vaccine Safety Datalink differ?
back: VAERS is passive, open reporting for rapid signal detection with no denominators or causality; the Vaccine Safety Datalink tests those signals against comparison groups in health system records.

front: Summarize the fate of the 1998 MMR-autism paper.
back: The 12-child Lancet case series was shown to involve undisclosed litigation funding and falsified histories, was fully retracted in 2010, its author lost his license, and controlled studies exceeding 650,000 children found no association.

front: How does nirsevimab differ from palivizumab?
back: Nirsevimab binds prefusion F with higher potency and carries half-life-extending Fc mutations, so one dose protects a full RSV season, replacing palivizumab's monthly high-risk-only dosing.

front: What anti-HBs level defines hepatitis B protection, and what does later waning mean in a documented responder?
back: Anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or higher after the series defines response; documented responders remain protected by memory B cells even after titers wane, needing no boosters or immune globulin.
